Stiff person syndrome masquerading as multiple sclerosis
Joseph J. Sabatino Jr a,b, Scott D. Newsome a,⁎
a Department of Neurology, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, USA
b University of California San Francisco, Department of Neurology, 1500 Owens St. Suite 320, San Francisco, CA 94158, USA

Received in revised form 8 November 2016
Accepted 28 November 2016
Available online 30 November 2016
Background:Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neuroimmunological disorder presenting with a wide variety of
signs and symptoms that mimic neuro-inﬂammatory diseases, such as multiple sclerosis (MS), thus delaying di-
agnosis.
Methods: We performed a retrospective chart review of over 100 patients with SPS who were treated at Johns
Hopkins Hospital and identiﬁed ﬁve patients previously diagnosed with MS.
Results: Patients were female with a mean age of 53 years old (range 43 – 64). Mean time to SPS diagnosis was
5.5 years. They presented with typical SPS features (axial/leg spasms, torso rigidity, hyperlordosis, and gait insta-
bility) as well as atypical features (hemiparesis, hemisensory dysfunction,ﬁne motor impairment) and were all
initially given a diagnosis of MS. In all patients, brain MRI demonstrated non-speci ﬁc white matter lesions and
CSF was negative for intrathecal antibodies in the 4 out of 5 patients who underwent lumbar puncture. SPS diag-
nosis was supported by elevated anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65) antibodies in each patient. Two pa-
tients were treated with disease-modifying therapies for MS before being diagnosed with SPS. Following
diagnosis with SPS, the patients were treated with varying combinations of immunosuppressants and symptom-
atic therapies resulting in stabilization or improvement in four of the patients.
Conclusion:We presentﬁve patients with SPS, who were initially thought to have MS, including one patient treat-
ed with three different MS therapies due to“disease progression”. These cases demonstrate the need to consider
less common neuroimmunological disorders, such as SPS, especially in patients with atypical features for MS.

1. Introduction
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune or paraneoplastic
disorder that classically causes rigidity and spasms of the proximal and
axial muscles, gait dysfunction and falls. Continuous co-contraction of
agonist and antagonist muscles, which can be evident clinically even
in the absence of electrophysiologic ﬁndings (i.e. continuous motor
unit activity on EMG), can cause severe hyperlordosis and greatly hin-
der basic movements such as walking, bending at the waist, and chest
movement during breathing [1]. SPS is typically associated with auto-
antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase 65 (GAD65)[1] though
other less common auto-antibodies have been linked to SPS as well.
There are also variants of SPS with atypical signs and symptoms includ-
ing rigidity and spasms of a single limb, ataxia, or progressive encepha-
lomyelitis and myoclonus[1,2]. In addition, SPS patients may have other
seemingly unrelated neurologic symptoms as well as anxiety and pho-
bias. Consequently, SPS often goes undiagnosed or misdiagnosed for
years. We describe a case series of patients with a diagnosis of SPS
who were previously diagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS).
2. Materials and methods
We performed a retrospective chart review of over 100 patients with
SPS who were treated at Johns Hopkins Hospital from 1996 to 2016 and
identiﬁed ﬁve patients previously diagnosed with MS. A diagnosis of SPS
was given based on prototypic exam ﬁndings (axial and/or limb stiff-
ness and rigidity, episodic spasms, and lumbar hyperlordosis), elevated
anti-GAD65 antibodies, and response to treatment. All review was done
in accordance with the IRB-approved protocol. Detailed pertinent de-
mographic, medical, and treatment history is outlined in Table 1.
3. Results

muscle spasms and rigidity. Exam was additionally notable for
hypomimia, dysarthria, mild proximal left-sided weakness and
dysmetria with a slow unsteady gait. MRI brain revealed scattered
non-enhancing T2 hyperintense subcortical lesions and mild global at-
